summary: Introduces bioctal, an alternative to hexadecimal designed to reduce mental effort when a number must be converted to binary by a person. It argues hexadecimal was chosen for four-bit groups but ignores cognitive factors. It is experimental, and appears to be in a humorous spirit.

plainLanguage.summary: A new way of writing numbers with fresh symbols, so people find it easier to turn into ones and zeros.

subtitle: An April Fools' proposal to replace hexadecimal with a more cognitive-friendly base-16 notation.

tldr.problem: Hexadecimal uses the letters A-F arbitrarily and requires mental effort to convert to binary, especially for digits in the middle of the range like C and D.
tldr.mechanism: This April Fools' RFC proposes Bioctal, which replaces hexadecimal digits 8-F with letters (c, j, z, w, f, s, b, v) chosen for their shapes, so the high bit in the second octave is obvious, reducing mental conversion overhead.
tldr.outcome: This is a humorous April 1st document published in 2022 that satirizes cognitive psychology applied to number systems.

facts.label: Second octave letters
facts.value: c, j, z, w, f, s, b, v

today: RFC 9226 is an Experimental RFC published on April 1, 2022, as an April Fools' Day joke. It is not a real notation system and was never intended for actual adoption in networks or computing.

sections.title: Problems with Hexadecimal
sections.content:
RFC 9226 proposes Bioctal as an alternative to hexadecimal for representing groups of four binary digits. The RFC argues that hexadecimal's alphabet (0-9, then A-F) is arbitrary: after exhausting decimal digits, it simply takes the first six letters. Converting a hexadecimal digit like "D" to binary requires remembering that D is 13, subtracting eight to get the octal range, then converting the result to binary—three mental operations instead of one.

The RFC invokes cognitive psychology's "seven plus or minus two" principle, suggesting octal (9 symbols) is within human working memory capacity while hexadecimal (16 symbols) is not. It notes that hexadecimal also contains two vowels, creating unfortunate collisions with words offensive to vegetarians and other groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Hexadecimal is hard because you have to remember what A, B, C, D, E, F mean, and then convert them to binary in your head. It is annoying.

sections.title: The Bioctal Alphabet
sections.content:
Bioctal replaces the second octave (8-F) with letters chosen for their shapes. The high bit (the most significant of four bits) follows a morphological mnemonic: 8→c, 9→j, A→z, B→w, C→f, D→s, E→b, F→v. For example, "2" has a curved top, and the uppercase letter "Z" echoes that shape; "5" has a horizontal line at top and bottom, and "S" mirrors that; "6" has a round bottom, and "b" reflects it. Choosing 'c' and 'j' for 0 and 1 avoids vowels and the confusable lowercase 'L'.

With Bioctal, identifying the high bit is trivial: if the digit is a letter, the high bit is 1; the remaining three bits are the same as for the Arabic numeral with the same shape. This eliminates the mental conversion penalty.
sections.plainLanguage: The new letters look like the numbers below them. If you see a letter, the top bit is 1. If you see a number, the top bit is 0. That is it.

sections.title: Objections and Defenses
sections.content: The RFC preemptively dismisses three objections. First, "bioctal" is already used for something else (combining two octal characters on paper tape), but the RFC argues the new meaning is superior and should displace the old. Second, some say hexadecimal is too entrenched to change, but the RFC retorts that technicians who cannot learn Bioctal should be "reassigned to duties involving only binary numbers." Third, Bioctal numbers do not sort numerically by ASCII order, but the RFC suggests they may sort naturally in "some lesser known variety of EBCDIC" and notes that resistance to numeric sorting "may be an indicator of virtue."
sections.plainLanguage: People will say hexadecimal is too old to change. The RFC says, "Too bad; if you do not like Bioctal, you can just use binary forever."

sections.title: Security and Implementation
sections.content: The RFC includes a Security Considerations section describing a contrived scenario involving a miniature lizard detector wristwatch where confusion between bioctal 'b' and hexadecimal 'B' causes a lizard detection subsystem to output hex when bioctal is expected, resulting in displaying "NL" (No Lizards) when it should display "KO" (Komodo dragon). The RFC notes this may be prejudicial to user security. Extensive research has uncovered no other security scenarios. The RFC also mentions that not all computers support lowercase letters, but observes that many machines with uppercase-only keyboards still support lowercase in practice, and uppercase Bioctal letters work (with extra mental cycles required for 'B').
sections.plainLanguage: The only security problem is if you mix Bioctal and hexadecimal by accident. The RFC uses a silly example with a lizard detector to illustrate this.
